concepts.name: Sensory Receptors
concepts.description: Learners should identify where and how organisms detect environmental stimuli.
concepts.evidence: Information from the environment is detected by specialised tips of nerve cells called receptors, located in the sense organs: the inner ear, the nose, the tongue, the eyes and the skin.

concepts.name: Neuron Structure
concepts.description: Learners should know the three main parts of a neuron and their functions.
concepts.evidence: A neuron, or nerve cell, has three parts: dendrites, which acquire information; the cell body; and the axon, a long extension along which information travels as an electrical impulse.

concepts.name: Synaptic Transmission
concepts.description: Learners should understand how an electrical impulse triggers chemical release across a synapse.
concepts.evidence: At the end of the axon, the electrical impulse sets off the release of chemicals, which cross a small gap called the synapse and start a similar electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron.

concepts.name: Reflex Arc
concepts.description: Learners should describe the pathway that produces a rapid involuntary response.
concepts.evidence: Nerves that detect heat are connected to nerves that move muscles, and this pathway, from the input nerve to the output nerve through the spinal cord, is called a reflex arc.

concepts.name: Brain Regions
concepts.description: Learners should identify the three major parts of the brain.
concepts.evidence: The brain has three major parts: the fore-brain, the mid-brain and the hind-brain.

concepts.name: Cerebellum Function
concepts.description: Learners should explain the role of the cerebellum in coordinating voluntary movements and balance.
concepts.evidence: The cerebellum, also in the hind-brain, is responsible for precision of voluntary actions and for maintaining posture and balance, such as walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle or picking up a pencil.

concepts.name: Plant Tropisms
concepts.description: Learners should recognize different growth‑directed movements of plants toward stimuli.
concepts.evidence: Shoots bend towards light (phototropism); roots grow downwards towards the pull of the earth (geotropism, or gravitropism) and towards water (hydrotropism); and pollen tubes grow towards ovules (chemotropism).

concepts.name: Auxin Mechanism
concepts.description: Learners should understand how auxin distribution causes phototropic bending.
concepts.evidence: When light comes from one side, auxin diffuses towards the shady side of the shoot, which stimulates the cells there to grow longer, so the shoot bends towards light.

concepts.name: Animal Hormones
concepts.description: Learners should define hormones as chemical messengers released by endocrine glands into the blood.
concepts.evidence: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood, which carries them to target organs.

concepts.name: Hormonal Feedback
concepts.description: Learners should describe how hormone release is regulated by feedback mechanisms.
concepts.evidence: The timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by feedback mechanisms: for example, if sugar levels in the blood rise, the cells of the pancreas detect it and produce more insulin, and as the sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced.

concepts.name: Muscle Contraction
concepts.description: Learners should explain how nervous impulses cause muscle fibers to shorten.
concepts.evidence: Muscle cells contain special proteins that change their shape and arrangement in response to nervous electrical impulses, which makes the muscle cells shorter.
